did_you_know.text: Did you know? Asa is explicitly described as doing what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God—a clear moral assessment at the beginning of the account of his reign.

Did you know? As part of a religious reform, Asa removed from Judah the altars of foreign gods and the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah poles—symbols and centers associated with idolatrous worship.
Did you know? Asa did not stop at removing these symbols; he commanded Judah to seek the LORD and to observe the law and the commandments.
Did you know? After the high places and sun-pillars were removed from the cities of Judah, the text describes the kingdom as being at peace during Asa’s reign.
Did you know? During this peaceful period, Asa built fortified cities, and the text connects the absence of war with the opportunity to strengthen the country’s defenses.
Did you know? The fortified cities included walls, towers, gates, and bars—a description that highlights the main defensive features of a fortified city in the biblical period.

Did you know? According to the text, Asa’s army consisted of 300,000 warriors from Judah, who carried large shields and spears, and another 280,000 from Benjamin, who carried shields and drew bows—a total of 580,000 men.
Did you know? Zerah the Cushite advanced as far as Mareshah at the head of a huge army of a thousand thousand—one million, according to the wording of the verse—and 300 chariots.
Did you know? The battle took place in the Valley of Zephathah, near Mareshah, and Asa went out to meet the Cushite army at the chosen battlefield.
Did you know? In his prayer before the battle, Asa emphasizes that the LORD can help whether there are many or those who have no strength, and declares that Judah relies on Him and comes in His name.
